clue.text: It's proverbially right to tear into a race

indicators.note: into says one piece goes inside the other, here the tearing word sits within the race

parts.note: the TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle race on the Isle of Man
to rive is an old word for to tear or split apart

explanation.surface: Someone claims an old saying approves of ripping into a race.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'as right as a trivet' explains the definition: a three-legged stand sits steady on any surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'right as a trivet' means perfectly fine, because a three-legged stand never wobbles.

clue.text: Pilot circling is able to climb and goes through the drama again

indicators.note: in a down entry climbing means reading upwards, so the whole assembly is written backwards
circling means the pilot word goes round the able word

parts.note: to pilot a vessel is to steer it
is able means can

explanation.surface: An aviator able to loop and climb performs the stunt again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pilot' suggests an airman but means to steer. 'To climb' signals reading upwards, as this is a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A group repeating a play or historical scene acts it out afresh.

clue.text: Confirm appointment after hearing of depression

indicators.note: hearing of means the word for depression is said out loud

parts.note: a valley is a depression in the land
a date is an arranged meeting

explanation.surface: A medical appointment confirmed after a hearing about depression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the appointment after the sound; 'depression' tempts a mental-health reading but is a dip in the land.
explanation.definitionFit: Validating something makes it officially sound, establishing it as true or genuine.

clue.text: Out West make do with variety show

indicators.note: variety says the letters are rearranged in a varied order
out tells us the letter for West leaves the word with

explanation.surface: In the Wild West they get by with a music-hall show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out West' removes W from WITH, leaving ITH; ITH and MAKEDO are rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mikado is a Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera, a stage production.

clue.text: Leading light in staff is Jack

parts.note: a pole is a long staff or rod
is shortened to 's gives S
a jack tar, or just a tar, is a sailor

explanation.surface: A guiding figure among the employees turns out to be someone called Jack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' reads as employees and 'Jack' as a man's name; in fact they are a rod and a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pole Star guides navigators, so figuratively it is a guiding principle or person.

clue.text: Regress, as we do once a year

definitions.text: as we do once a year

explanation.surface: Go backwards, as everyone does each year.
explanation.walkthrough: In autumn clocks go back an hour at the end of summer time.
explanation.definitionFit: To return to old ways is idiomatically to undo progress, and literally the hour changes back in autumn.

clue.text: Beryl, a Cockney border official

indicators.note: a Cockney speaker drops initial h sounds, so both words lose their H

parts.note: a hem is the border of a garment
a herald is an officer of arms

explanation.surface: Beryl, a London lady, works as a frontier officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beryl' poses as a woman's name. The Cockney accent turns HEM HERALD into 'EM 'ERALD.
explanation.definitionFit: The green gemstone is a variety of the mineral beryl.

clue.text: A variety of tuberose. I admit

indicators.note: a variety of suggests the letters of the flower are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone concedes the plant is a kind of tuberose.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase concedes a point, like granted or certainly.

clue.text: Not Oxbridge material

parts.note: reads as an unsuitable applicant to Oxford or Cambridge, but means the building material of newer universities, which are not the ancient two

explanation.surface: A student judged not good enough for Oxford or Cambridge.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxbridge means Oxford and Cambridge; the 'redbrick' universities founded in industrial cities were built of brick, unlike the old stone colleges.
explanation.definitionFit: Redbrick universities are later British foundations, contrasted with Oxford and Cambridge, and named for their building material.

clue.text: Determined man will be not disheartened

parts.note: a man will is he will, shortened to he'll
taken as written

indicators.note: with its heart removed only the first and last letters of the word not remain

explanation.surface: A resolute man vows he will not lose heart.
explanation.definitionFit: Being set on something at any cost is to be utterly resolved, as in 'hell-bent on revenge'.

clue.text: In a trap, Welsh retreated

parts.note: the tide ebbed when it went back out, so ebbed means retreated

explanation.surface: Caught in an ambush, the Welsh troops fell back.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads the answer as 'caught in a web', so a trap.
explanation.definitionFit: Something caught in a web is snared, the spider's net acting as the snare.

clue.text: Old port and a bit to eat

explanation.surface: An ancient harbour town and a snack.
explanation.walkthrough: SANDWICH in Kent was one of the medieval Cinque Ports; its harbour has long silted up, hence 'old'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kentish town was once a leading Cinque Port, and the snack of filling between bread slices is named after an Earl of the town.

clue.text: A shrew forced into line

indicators.note: the letters of a shrew are forced into a new shape

explanation.surface: A nagging woman is forced to fall into line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Into' is a link joining the anagram to the definition, not a container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A hawser is a thick rope or cable used for mooring or towing ships.

clue.text: Put a roof on the more distant church, man

parts.note: that points to the further of two things, as against this
Ed is a short form of a man's name, Edward

explanation.surface: Roof over the church that is further away, mate.
explanation.definitionFit: Thatching means covering a building's top with straw or reeds.

clue.text: Grenadine used in making sweet

indicators.note: the letters of the syrup are used to make something new

explanation.surface: Grenadine syrup is used in making a confection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' looks like a dessert but is an adjective, meaning charming.
explanation.definitionFit: Something endearing is lovable and charming, which is a sense of sweet.

clue.text: After 6 in Ireland you need a key

explanation.surface: Next to a precious stone in Ireland you must carry a key.
explanation.walkthrough: 6 down is EMERALD, and 'the Emerald Isle' is Ireland. A key (or cay) is a low island, as in the Florida Keys.
explanation.definitionFit: Ireland is nicknamed the Emerald Isle, and a key is a small low island or reef.

clue.text: Grouse may be secure

explanation.surface: Game birds may be safely caught.
explanation.walkthrough: Shot game is put in the game bag, so a grouse 'in the bag' has been shot.
explanation.definitionFit: Shot game birds go into a bag, and an outcome already assured is said to be certain.

clue.text: I need to think, and I want to look

explanation.surface: A person pauses to ponder, then asks to see.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is said when pausing to ponder, and also when asking for a glimpse of something.

clue.text: Eat a little, or a lot

explanation.surface: Nibble, or gorge yourself.
explanation.definitionFit: To nibble at food is to peck at it, and in 'a peck of trouble' the word means a great deal.

clue.text: One inside is more likely to appear outside

indicators.note: to appear outside means the comparative word wraps around the little word is

parts.note: prone means likely, so more likely is proner
taken as written

explanation.surface: A remark that someone indoors is likelier to be seen out of doors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One inside' is slang for a jailed person, with 'outside' as its playful opposite in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone held in jail is said to be inside.

clue.text: City only half planned — in the early stages they tolerated anything

indicators.note: only the first half of the word for planned is kept

parts.note: calculated means carefully planned

indicators.note: the starting letters of three words are taken

explanation.surface: A city only half laid out, where at first anything was allowed.
explanation.walkthrough: Halving CALCULATED leaves CALCU; the opening letters of 'they tolerated anything' give TTA.
explanation.definitionFit: Calcutta, now Kolkata, is a major city in eastern India.

clue.text: It's not surprising these days on the 25

parts.note: now means at the present time
taken as written
25 across is GERMAN, and der is German for the

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that nothing is surprising on the 25th nowadays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The 25' looks like a date but means 'the' in German, from 25 across.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom saying something is only to be expected.

clue.text: Legal term in England but, strangely, not in US

indicators.note: strangely says the letters of the phrase are put in an odd order

explanation.surface: A legal word used in England but, oddly, not in America.
explanation.walkthrough: A nonsuit is the dismissal of a case when the plaintiff fails to make one out.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonsuit is a court's dismissal of a claim for want of evidence, a legal term.

clue.text: Kind chap's wearing a shade

indicators.note: something wearing a garment is inside it, so the chap goes inside the shade

parts.note: a hue is a shade of colour
a chap is a man; the 's is a link meaning is

explanation.surface: A benevolent fellow is wearing sunglasses or a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Being humane means acting with compassion and gentleness, a synonym of being kind.

clue.text: Carrier hit back with half the guns

indicators.note: back signals that the word for hit is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: to spank is to hit with a slap

indicators.note: only the first half of the anti-aircraft gun word is kept

parts.note: ack-ack is slang for anti-aircraft guns

explanation.surface: A gun carrier strikes back with half its artillery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' turns SPANK into KNAPS; ack-ack is wartime slang for anti-aircraft fire.
explanation.definitionFit: A knapsack is a bag carried on the back, so a carrier of gear.

clue.text: Pyrenean garment

explanation.surface: A piece of clothing from the mountains between France and Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: The Basque people live in the western Pyrenees, and a basque is a close-fitting bodice.

clue.text: Transfer 25, say, to eight, say

parts.note: a German, from 25 across, is an example of a foreigner or alien

indicators.note: say here means the word eight is spoken, giving its sound

parts.note: the number eight is pronounced the same as the past tense of eat

explanation.surface: Moving the 25th to the eighth, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: In law to alienate property is to transfer its ownership to another.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, alienating land or rights means conveying ownership to another party.

clue.text: Extinct creature spoken of in gloomy discussion

indicators.note: spoken of signals that the answer sounds like the phrase that follows

parts.note: a gloomy, dull discussion is grey talk

explanation.surface: A vanished species gets mentioned in a dismal debate.
explanation.definitionFit: The great auk was a flightless seabird hunted to extinction in the 1840s.

clue.text: European composer

explanation.surface: A continental musician.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward German was an English composer of light opera, best known for Merrie England.
explanation.definitionFit: A citizen of Germany is a European, and Sir Edward German wrote light operas.
